claims.claim: 18 lake populations (Great Lakes-basin winters): 60 mm proposed minimum (for first-winter survival)
claims.location: p. iv (PDF p. 6), Abstract; p. 32 (PDF p. 60), Ch. III abstract; p. 98 (PDF p. 126), §3.5 Discussion
claims.quote: a threshold of 60 mm can be identified as the minimum body length required
claims.conditions: age-0 yellow perch, 18 lake populations (Ch. III: 17 lakes or basins in three lake-size classes), 1958–1998 cohorts; size-selective survival inferred from autumn-to-spring length-frequency changes and otolith back-calculated end-of-season lengths; TOTAL length; the 60 mm is drawn 'when these two studies are taken together' with Post & Evans (1989, 57 mm)
claims.note: Now verified in the full text: drop '(relayed by a search summary; unverified)'. It is a soft threshold, not a cliff: 'equal to or greater than about 60 mm ... in most lakes were observed to have a greater likelihood of survival' (p. 98), and Ch. III 'generally identified 60 mm as the minimum total body length' (p. 32). Add 'TL'.

claims.quote: generally identified 60 mm as the minimum total body length required for survival
claims.note: The same page credits Post & Evans (1989) with 57 mm (p. 98).

notes: Scanned thesis (no text layer); read on page images: the title page, the thesis abstract (pp. iii–iv), the contents (pp. x–xii), Ch. III's abstract (pp. 32–33) and its discussion of overwinter survival (pp. 90–99), and the start of the general discussion (pp. 207–210). The verdict is 'corrected' only for the URL; the claim checks. Other points: the thesis argues age-0 perch growth is similar across lakes of very different size (length-by-date overlap), and links strong year classes to adults' asynchronous spawning in the 1998 El Niño spring; it says distinguishing starvation from predation as the cause of winter loss 'requires further study' (p. iv).
